                    ### Question
                    A 22-year-old female presents at 24 weeks gestation with a chief complaint of burning upon urination. On physical exam, you note a gravid uterus that extends above the umbilicus. A urine analysis and culture is sent demonstrating over 100,000 colony forming units of E. coli. Of note this patient had a similar UTI 7 weeks ago that was resolved with appropriate medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Nitrofurantoin
opb. TMP-SMX
opc. Cephalexin
opd. Nitrofurantoin and continue with nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for the rest of the pregnancy
ope. Cephalexin and IV antibiotic prophylaxis for the rest of the pregnancy

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
A 22-year-old female at 24 weeks gestation presents with burning upon urination and a urine culture showing >100,000 CFU of E. coli, indicating a urinary tract infection (UTI). Given her history of a similar UTI 7 weeks ago, there is a risk of recurrent infections. In pregnancy, the choice of antibiotics must prioritize safety for both the mother and fetus. Nitrofurantoin and Cephalexin are both considered safe options for treating UTIs in pregnancy, while Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is less preferred, especially in the third trimester due to potential risks. Prophylaxis may be warranted due to her recurrent UTIs. Therefore, the most appropriate management is Nitrofurantoin, with the option to continue prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy, as it is effective and safe. This aligns with current medical consensus on UTI management in pregnant patients.
